about: Real papers (by DOI) and the evidence category each should receive against a claim, judged from the paper's abstract as retrieved from Europe PMC on 6 November 2026. Labelled by Claude (an AI), not by a subject expert: treat as a first check, to be reviewed by a researcher. Abstracts are fetched at run time and not stored here. Papers whose label was not clear-cut from the abstract were left out.

claims.learning_styles: Matching instruction to students' learning styles improves learning outcomes.
claims.bednets: Insecticide-treated nets reduce malaria in children.
claims.retrieval: Retrieval practice improves long-term retention compared with restudying.
claims.vitd_cancer: Vitamin D supplementation reduces cancer incidence.

items.why: Describes VARK preferences; no test of matched instruction.
Learning styles and reaction time; no learning outcome of matching.
Meta-analysis: small overall benefit (g = 0.31) but only 26% of outcomes show the crossover the hypothesis needs, low study quality.
Experiment: instruction matched to style preference did not improve learning.
Review of rigorous studies: effect sizes very low and non-significant; no replicable evidence.
Effect of malaria infection on anaemia; nets not the exposure.
Modelling of the RTS,S vaccine.
Vaccine introduction; net coverage is only a baseline characteristic.
Climate-change interventions for child health in general.
Retrieval practice beat repeated studying on 30- and 50-day recognition tests.
Testing effect shown, but only 15 minutes later: no long-term measure.
Retrieval scores correlate with exam scores; no comparison with restudying.
AI-assisted versus traditional learning, not retrieval practice versus restudying.
Narrative review: whether vitamin D affects cancer risk in BRCA1 carriers remains unclear.
Vitamin D and oral health.
Omega-3 during chemotherapy; treatment outcomes, not cancer incidence.
Infection-related hospitalisations.
Thyroid disorders.
NK-cell biology in pancreatic cancer; no supplementation and incidence.
Observational: supplementation associated with lower hepatobiliary malignancy risk in PSC patients.
